page: Amazon Web Services m6g.xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine instance powered by custom 64-bit ARM-based AWS Graviton2 processors. It features 4 dedicated physical cores utilizing the ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 microarchitecture running at 2.5 GHz, with 1.0 thread per core. The instance is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per core. It operates on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, does not include local NVMe storage, and has a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. No GPU accelerators are present on this hardware profile.

In benchmark evaluations, the m6g.xlarge demonstrates moderate compute capabilities. Its stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU performance fall within the average range, scoring 1519.69 and 6053.37 respectively. Large-block memory bandwidth benchmarks also show average performance, with read speeds of 71.67 GB/sec and write speeds of 34.85 GB/sec. However, the instance exhibits weaker performance in memory-bound and single-threaded tasks, as evidenced by a weak Geekbench single-core score of 962.0 and a poor Passmark CPU score of 2686.24. Cryptographic performance is supported by hardware-accelerated AES, though the architecture lacks x86-specific instruction sets like AVX or AMX.

Given its balanced resource allocation, the m6g.xlarge is designed for general-purpose workloads that benefit from dedicated ARM cores. It is suited for applications such as application servers, mid-size database operations, caching fleets, and microservices. The ARM64 architecture offers qualitative cost efficiency by delivering reliable multi-core performance and dedicated resource allocation at a lower resource-to-cost profile compared to traditional x86 architectures, though workloads requiring high single-threaded throughput or specialized vector instructions may experience performance tradeoffs.
description: Amazon Web Services m6g.xlarge is a general-purpose instance powered by a 2.5 GHz AWS Graviton2 processor with 4 dedicated ARM64 physical cores and 16.0 GB of RAM. Built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, it provides a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio but lacks local storage and GPU acceleration. Performance benchmarks indicate average capabilities in multi-core processing and large-block memory bandwidth, though it exhibits weaker single-threaded and cryptographic execution compared to x86 alternatives. The instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for multi-threaded workloads, making it suitable for application servers, containerized microservices, and moderate database operations that can leverage the ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 architecture.
